Coptic Orthodox Church
The Coptic Orthodox Church, also known as the Coptic Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria, is an <color=#3366CC>Oriental Orthodox</color>
<color=#3366CC>Christian</color> church based in <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>. The head of the Coptic Orthodox Church and of the See of <color=#3366CC>Alexandria</color> is the pope of
Alexandria on the Holy Apostolic See of <color=#3366CC>Saint Mark</color>. The current pope of the Coptic Orthodox Church is Pope
Tawadros II. (Coptic: II) The See of Alexandria is titular. The Coptic pope presides from Saint Mark's Coptic Orthodox
Cathedral in the Abbassia district in <color=#3366CC>Cairo</color>. The church follows the Coptic Rite for its liturgy, prayer and devotional
patrimony. Adherents of the Coptic Orthodox Church make up Egypt's largest and most significant minority population,
and the largest population of Christians in the <color=#3366CC>Middle East and North Africa (MENA)</color>. They make up the largest share of
the approximately 10 million Christians in Egypt.
According to Coptic tradition, the Coptic Orthodox Church was established by Saint Mark the Evangelist, a companion
of the Apostles, during the middle of the 1st century (c. AD 42). Due to disputes concerning the nature of Christ, the
Oriental Orthodox Churches were in schism after the <color=#3366CC>Council of Chalcedon</color> in AD 451.
After AD 639, Egypt was ruled by its <color=#3366CC>Islamic</color> conquerors from <color=#3366CC>Arabia</color>. In the 12th century, the church relocated its seat
from Alexandria to Cairo. The same century also saw the <color=#3366CC>Copts</color> become a religious minority. During the 14th and 15th
centuries, Nubian Christianity was supplanted by Islam. In the 19th and 20th centuries, the larger body of ethnic
Egyptian Christians began to call themselves Coptic Orthodox, to distinguish themselves from the Catholic Copts and
from the Eastern Orthodox, who are mostly Greek. In 1959, the <color=#3366CC>Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church</color> was granted
autocephaly. This was extended to the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church in 1998 following the successful <color=#3366CC>Eritrean</color>
<color=#3366CC>War of Independence</color> from <color=#3366CC>Ethiopia</color>.
History
Apostolic foundation
According to tradition, the Coptic Church was founded by St. <color=#3366CC>Mark the Evangelist</color> c. AD 42; it regards itself as the
subject of many <color=#3366CC>prophecies</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Old Testament</color>.
Coptic language in the church
The <color=#3366CC>Coptic language</color> is a universal language used in Coptic churches in every country. It descends from <color=#3366CC>Ancient</color>
<color=#3366CC>Egyptian</color> and uses the Coptic alphabet, a script descended from the <color=#3366CC>Greek alphabet</color> with added characters derived
from the Demotic script. Today, the Bohairic dialect of Coptic is used primarily for liturgical purposes. Many of the
hymns in the liturgy are in Coptic and have been passed down for many centuries. The language is used to preserve
Egypt's dominant language prior to the <color=#3366CC>Arab conquest</color>, after which Coptic was banned by Arab rulers and gradually
supplanted by Arabic. Today, most Copts speak <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color> as their first language, the official language of Egypt. Hence,
Arabic is also used in church services nowadays. The service books, though written in Coptic, have Arabic text in
parallel columns.
Catechetical School of Alexandria
The Catechetical School of Alexandria is the oldest catechetical school in the world. <color=#3366CC>Jerome</color> records that the Christian
School of Alexandria was founded by Mark himself.
The theological college of the catechetical school was re-established in 1893.
The school became a leading center of the allegorical method of biblical interpretation, espoused rapprochement
between Greek culture and the Christian faith, and attempted to assert orthodox Christian teachings against heterodox
views in an era of doctrinal flux.
Role and participation in the ecumenical councils
Council of Nicaea
In the 4th century, an Alexandrian presbyter named <color=#3366CC>Arius</color> began a theological dispute about the nature of Christ that
spread throughout the Christian world and is now known as <color=#3366CC>Arianism</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Council of Nicea</color> in AD 325 was convened
by <color=#3366CC>Emperor Constantine I</color> after Pope Alexander I of Alexandria proposed holding a council to respond to heresies. A
council under the presidency of <color=#3366CC>Hosius of Cordova</color> attempted to resolve the dispute. This eventually led to the
formulation of the Symbol of Faith, also known as the <color=#3366CC>Nicene Creed</color>.
Council of Constantinople
In AD 381, Pope Timothy I of Alexandria presided over the second ecumenical council known as the First Council of
Constantinople, to judge Macedonius, who denied the Divinity of the Holy Spirit. This council completed the <color=#3366CC>Nicene</color>
<color=#3366CC>Creed</color> with this confirmation of the divinity of the <color=#3366CC>Holy Spirit</color>:
We believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the Giver of Life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the
Son is worshiped and glorified who spoke by the Prophets and in One, Holy, Catholic, and Apostolic church. We
confess one Baptism for the remission of sins and we look for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the coming
age, Amen
Council of Ephesus
Another theological dispute in the 5th century occurred over the teachings of <color=#3366CC>Nestorius</color>, the patriarch of Constantinople
who taught that God the Word was not hypostatically joined with human nature, but rather dwelt in the man Jesus. As a
consequence of this, he denied the title "Mother of God" (Theotokos) to the <color=#3366CC>Virgin Mary</color>, declaring her instead to be
"Mother of Christ" Christotokos.
The council confirmed the teachings of <color=#3366CC>Athanasius</color> and confirmed the title of Mary as "Mother of God". It also clearly
stated that anyone who separated Christ into two hypostases was anathema, as Cyril had said that there is "One
Nature for God the Word Incarnate" (Mia Physis tou Theou Logou Sesarkōmenē). The introduction to the creed is
formulated as follows:
We magnify you O Mother of the True Light and we glorify you O saint and Mother of God (Theotokos) for you have
borne unto us the Saviour of the world. Glory to you O our Master and King: Christ, the pride of the Apostles, the crown
of the martyrs, the rejoicing of the righteous, firmness of the churches and the forgiveness of sins. We proclaim the
Holy Trinity in One Godhead: we worship Him, we glorify Him, Lord have mercy, Lord have mercy, Lord bless us,
Amen.
Council of Chalcedon
The church of Alexandria was part in communion with the rest of Christendom until the <color=#3366CC>Council of Chalcedon</color>. When, in
AD 451, Emperor Marcian attempted to heal divisions in the church, the response of Pope Dioscorus–the Pope of
Alexandria who was later exiled–was that the emperor should not intervene in the affairs of the church. It was at
Chalcedon that the emperor, through the imperial delegates, enforced harsh disciplinary measures against Pope
Dioscorus in response to his boldness. In AD 449, Pope Dioscorus headed the 2nd Council of Ephesus, called the
"Robber Council" by Chalcedonian historians. It held to the Miaphysite formula which upheld the Christology of "One
Incarnate Nature of God the Word" (Ancient Greek: mia physis Theou Logou sesarkōmenē).
In terms of Christology, the <color=#3366CC>Oriental Orthodox</color> (Non-Chalcedonians) understanding is that Christ is "One Nature—the
Logos Incarnate," of the full humanity and full divinity. The Chalcedonians' understanding is that Christ is recognized in
two natures, full humanity and full divinity. Oriental Orthodoxy contends that such a formulation is no different from what
the Nestorians teach.
From that point onward, Alexandria would have two patriarchs: the non-Chalcedonian native Egyptian one, now known
as the Coptic pope of Alexandria and patriarch of All Africa on the Holy Apostolic See of St. Mark, and the Melkite or
Imperial patriarch, now known as the Greek Orthodox patriarch of Alexandria.
Almost the entire Egyptian population rejected the terms of the Council of Chalcedon and remained faithful to the native
Egyptian Church (now known as the Coptic Orthodox Church).
By anathematizing Pope Leo because of the tone and content of his tome, as per Alexandrine Theology perception,
Pope Dioscorus was found guilty of doing so without due process; in other words, the Tome of Leo was not a subject of
heresy in the first place, but it was a question of questioning the reasons behind not having it either acknowledged or
read at the Second Council of Ephesus in AD 449. Pope Dioscorus of Alexandria was never labeled as a heretic by the
council's canons. Copts also believe that the pope of Alexandria was forcibly prevented from attending the third
congregation of the council from which he was ousted, apparently the result of a conspiracy tailored by the Roman
delegates.
Before the current positive era of Eastern and Oriental Orthodox dialogues, Chalcedonians sometimes used to call the
non-Chalcedonians "Monophysites", though the Coptic Orthodox Church in reality regards Monophysitism as a heresy.
The Chalcedonian doctrine in turn came to be known as "Dyophysite". A term that comes closer to Coptic Orthodoxy is
Miaphysite, which refers to a conjoined nature for Christ, both human and divine, united indivisibly in the Incarnate
Logos.
From Chalcedon to the Arab conquest of Egypt
Muslim conquest of Egypt
The <color=#3366CC>Muslim invasion of Egypt</color> took place in AD 639. Relying on eyewitness testimony, Bishop John of Nikiu in his
Chronicle provides a graphic account of the invasion from a Coptic perspective. Although the Chronicle has only been
preserved in an Ethiopic (Ge'ez) text, some scholars believe that it was originally written in Coptic. John's account is
critical of the invaders who he says "despoiled the Egyptians of their possessions and dealt cruelly with them", and he
details the atrocities committed by the Muslims against the native population during the conquest:And when with great
toil and exertion they had cast down the walls of the city, they forthwith made themselves masters of it, and put to the
sword thousands of its inhabitants and of the soldiers, and they gained an enormous booty, and took the women and
children captive and divided them amongst themselves, and they made that city a desolation.
Though critical of the Muslim commander (<color=#3366CC>Amr ibn al-As</color>), who, during the campaign, he says "had no mercy on the
Egyptians, and did not observe the covenant they had made with him, for he was of a barbaric race", he does note that
following the completion of the conquest, Amr "took none of the property of the Churches, and he committed no act of
spoilation or plunder, and he preserved them throughout all his days."
Despite the political upheaval, the Egyptian population remained mainly Christian. However, gradual conversions to
<color=#3366CC>Islam</color> over the centuries had changed Egypt from a Christian to a largely Muslim country by the end of the 12th century.
Another scholar writes that a combination of "repression of Coptic revolts", Arab-Muslim immigration, and Coptic
conversion to Islam resulted in the demographic decline of the Copts. Egypt's Umayyad rulers taxed Christians at a
higher rate than Muslims, driving merchants towards Islam and undermining the economic base of the Coptic Church.
Although the Coptic Church did not disappear, the Umayyad tax policies made it difficult for the church to retain the
Egyptian elites.
Under Islamic rule (640–1800)
In 969, Egypt entered the <color=#3366CC>Fatimid</color> dynasty (in Egypt from 969 to 1171), who adopted a largely favorable attitude toward
the Christians. The major exception to this was the persecution led by Caliph al-Hakim between 1004 and 1013, which
included clothing regulations, prohibition of publicly celebrating Christian festivals, and dismissal of Christian and
Jewish functionaries. However, at the end of his reign al-Hakim rescinded these measures, allowing the Copts to regain
privileged positions within the administration.
The Coptic patriarchal residence moved from Alexandria to Cairo during the patriarchate of Cyril II (1078–92). This
move was at the demand of the grand vizier Badr al-Jamali, who insisted that the pope establish himself in the capital.
When Saladin entered Egypt in 1163, this ushered in a government focused on defending Sunni Islam. Christians were
again discriminated against, and meant to show modesty in their religious ceremonies and buildings.
During the Ottoman period, Copts were classified alongside other Oriental Orthodox and Nestorian peoples under the
Armenian millet.
In 1798, the French invaded Egypt unsuccessfully and the British helped the Turks to regain power over Egypt under
the Muhammad Ali dynasty.
From the 19th century to the 1952 revolution
The position of Copts began to improve early in the 19th century under the stability and tolerance of the <color=#3366CC>Muhammad Ali</color>
<color=#3366CC>Dynasty</color>. The Coptic community ceased to be regarded by the state as an administrative unit. In 1855 the jizya tax was
abolished by Sa'id Pasha. Shortly thereafter, the Copts started to serve in the Egyptian army.
Towards the end of the 19th century, the Coptic Church underwent phases of new development. In 1853, Pope Cyril IV
established the first modern Coptic schools, including the first Egyptian school for girls. He also founded a printing
press, which was only the second national press in the country. The pope established very friendly relations with other
denominations, to the extent that when the Greek Patriarch in Egypt had to absent himself from the country for a long
period of time, he left his church under the guidance of the Coptic patriarch.
The Theological College of the School of Alexandria was reestablished in 1893. It began its new history with five
students, one of whom was later to become its dean. Today it has campuses in Alexandria and Cairo, and in various
dioceses throughout Egypt, as well as outside Egypt. It has campuses in New Jersey, Los Angeles, Sydney,
Melbourne, and London, where potential clergymen and other qualified men and women study many subjects, including
theology, church history, missionary studies, and the Coptic language.
From the mid 20th to the early 21st centuries
In 1959, the <color=#3366CC>Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church</color> was granted its first own patriarch Abuna Basilios by Pope Cyril VI.
Furthermore, the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church similarly became independent of the Ethiopian Orthodox
Tewahedo Church in 1994, when four bishops were consecrated by Pope Shenouda III of Alexandria to form the basis
of a local Holy Synod of the Eritrean Church. In 1998, the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church gained its autocephaly
from the Coptic Orthodox Church when its first patriarch was enthroned by Pope Shenouda III.
Since the 1980s theologians from the Oriental (non-Chalcedonian) Orthodox and Eastern (Chalcedonian) Orthodox
churches have been meeting in a bid to resolve theological differences, and have concluded that many of the
differences are caused by the two groups using different terminology to describe the same thing.
In the 1990s, the Orthodox Church of the British Isles (formerly the Catholicate of the West) joined the Coptic Orthodox
Church as a diocese named the British Orthodox Church. By 2015, it formally separated with the Coptic Orthodox
Church as a non-canonical, autocephalous church.
In the summer of 2001, the Coptic Orthodox and Greek Orthodox patriarchates of Alexandria agreed to mutually
recognize baptisms performed in each other's churches, making re-baptisms unnecessary, and to recognize the
sacrament of marriage as celebrated by the other.
In <color=#3366CC>Tahrir Square</color>, Cairo, on Wednesday 2 February 2011, Coptic Christians joined hands to provide a protective cordon
around their Muslim neighbors during <color=#3366CC>salat</color> (prayers) in the midst of the <color=#3366CC>2011 Egyptian Revolution</color>.
Continued persecution into the 21st century
While Copts have cited instances of persecution throughout their history, <color=#3366CC>Human Rights Watch</color> has noted growing
religious intolerance and sectarian violence against Coptic Christians in recent years, and a failure by the Egyptian
government to effectively investigate properly and prosecute those responsible. More than a hundred Egyptian copts
were killed in sectarian clashes from 2011 to 2017, and many homes and businesses destroyed. In <color=#3366CC>Minya</color>, 77 cases of
sectarian attacks on Copts between 2011 and 2016 were documented by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights.
Coptic Christian women and girls are often abducted and disappear.
In 2015, 21 men traveled to Libya to support their families. There, they would be kidnapped and beheaded by the
Islamic State in Libya.
Continued church reforms
Under Pope Shenouda III, from 1971 to 2012, the church underwent a large transformation. Writing in 2013, the
<color=#3366CC>theologian</color> Samuel Tadros stated "Today's Coptic Church as an institution is built solely on his vision". For the first time
in its history, the synod codified its internal laws. It also established numerous coptic institutions within and outside of
Egypt. Shenouda raised the number of bishops from 26 to 117 and ordained hundreds of priests, which greatly reduced
the influence of any one bishop. Shenouda also instituted a yearly meeting of the synod, which greatly expanded the
number of laws governing the church. This included instituting church curriculums for the education of new priests, new
deacons, and newly weds. For the first time in the Coptic Church's modern history, women could become ordained as
deacons. The synod also adopted a model for community development, dramatically increasing the scope of
community services provided by the church, including: hospitals, adult literacy schools, orphanages, libraries, and
community centres. Much of this work was fuelled by donations from wealthy Coptic industrialists and Copts from
abroad. Shenouda also held talks with the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches, in an effort to promote
ecumenism. On 10 May 1973, Shenouda visited the Vatican, where a joint Christological declaration was issued jointly
by the Coptic Orthodox and Catholic churches.
Pope Shenouda also increased the church's involvement in politics, seeing it as a way to advocate for the interest of
Copts, during the rise of Islamism in Egypt and increase in terrorist attacks. The president of Egypt, <color=#3366CC>Anwar Sadat</color>
ordered that Shenouda be put into exile in a Coptic Monastery far away from Cairo in 1981. This exile was short lived,
ending when Sadat was assassinated by Muslim extremists a few months later. Under president Hosni Mubarak,
Shenouda continued his political stance and often protested persecution of Copts by leaving Cairo and staying in
seclusion, which often caused the regime to quickly address issues. Shenouda's political involvement drew criticism
from some church members, including the prominent monk Father Matta El Meskeen.
On 17 March 2012, Pope Shenouda died, leaving many Copts mourning and worrying as tensions rose with <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color>.
Shenouda constantly met with Muslim leaders in order to create peace, his death resulting in concerns that without his
mediation good relations would break down. Many were worried about increased Islamic control of Egypt as the <color=#3366CC>Muslim</color>
<color=#3366CC>Brotherhood</color> won 70% of the parliamentary elections. Shenouda's approach to church leadership has, in part, been
adopted by the current patriarch. Pope Tawadros II of Alexandria maintains relations with the Egyptian government and
other churches. However, while Shenouda was critical of the expanded influence of Protestant teaching and books in
Coptic churches, Tawadros has increased ecumenical dialogue with several Protestant churches. In 2013, Tawadros
supported the movement demanding the removal of Egyptian Islamist president <color=#3366CC>Mohamed Morsi</color>. However, Tawadros
has been a relatively less political figure than his predecessor and has expressed support for the Egyptian
government's institutions during crises.
On 10 May 2023, Pope Tawadros visited the Vatican to celebrate Coptic-Catholic Friendship day and the 50 year
anniversary of the meeting between Pope Paul VI and Pope Shenouda III. In this same year Pope Francis announced
that the 21 Coptic Martyrs killed by ISIS in Libya in 2015 would be added to the Catholic Roman Martyrology, and Pope
Tawadros gifted relics from each of the 21 martyrs to the Vatican.
Fasts, feasts, liturgy and canonical hours
Communicants of the Coptic Orthodox Church use a breviary known as the Agpeya to pray the canonical hours at
seven fixed prayer times while facing in the eastward direction, in anticipation of the <color=#3366CC>Second Coming of Jesus</color>; this
Christian practice has its roots in Psalm 119:164, in which the prophet <color=#3366CC>David</color> prays to God seven times a day. Church
bells enjoin Christians to pray at these hours. Before praying, they wash their hands and face to be clean before and
present their best to God; shoes are removed to acknowledge that one is offering prayer before a holy God. During
each of the seven fixed prayer times, Coptic Orthodox Christians pray "prostrating three times in the name of the
<color=#3366CC>Trinity</color>; at the end of each Psalm ... while saying the 'Alleluia';" and 41 times for each of the Kyrie eleisons present in a
canonical hour. In the Coptic Orthodox Church, it is customary for women to wear a Christian headcovering when
praying. The Coptic Orthodox Church observes days of ritual purification. However, while meat that still contains blood
after cooking is discouraged from being eaten, the Coptic Church does not forbid its members from consuming any
particular type of food, unlike in Islam or <color=#3366CC>Judaism</color>.
All churches of the Coptic Orthodox Church are designed to face the eastward direction of prayer and efforts are made
to remodel churches obtained from other <color=#3366CC>Christian denominations</color> that are not built in this fashion.
In Coptic Orthodox Christianity, fasting is traditionally defined as going without water and food from midnight to sunset;
after that time, the consumption of water and one vegetarian meal is permitted. In addition to fasting, Coptic Christians
practice abstinence from meat, eggs, and lacticinia (milk, butter, and cheese) when preparing supper. With respect to
Eucharistic discipline, Coptic Orthodox Christians <color=#3366CC>fast</color> from midnight onwards (or at least nine hours) prior to receiving
the sacrament of <color=#3366CC>Holy Communion</color>. They fast every Wednesday and Friday of the year (Wednesdays in remembrance
of the betrayal of Christ, and on Fridays in remembrance of His crucifixion and death). In total, fast days in a year for
Coptic Orthodox Christians numbers between 210 and 240. This means that Copts abstain from all animal products for
up to two-thirds of each year. The fasts for <color=#3366CC>Advent</color> and <color=#3366CC>Lent</color> are 43 days and 55 days, respectively. In August, before
the celebration of the Dormition of the Mother of God, Coptic Christians fast 15 days; fasting is also done before the
feast of Feast of Saints Peter and Paul, starting from the day of <color=#3366CC>Pentecost</color>. Married couples refrain from sexual
relations during Lent "to give themselves time for fasting and prayer".
Christmas has been a national holiday in Egypt since 2003. It is the only Christian holiday in Egypt. Coptic Christmas,
which usually falls on January 6 or 7 is a major feast. Other major feasts are <color=#3366CC>Epiphany</color>, <color=#3366CC>Palm Sunday</color>, <color=#3366CC>Easter</color>,
Pentecost, Ascension, and Annunciation. These are known in the Coptic world as the Seven Major Feasts. Major feasts
are always preceded by fasts. Additionally, the Coptic Orthodox Church also has Seven Minor Feasts: the Circumcision
of the Lord, Entrance into the Temple, Entrance into Egypt, Transfiguration, Maundy Thursday, Thomas Sunday, and
Great Lent. Furthermore, there are several indigenous feasts of the Theotokos. There are also other feasts
commemorating the martyrdom of important saints from Coptic history.
Demographics
Available Egyptian census figures and other third-party survey reports have not reported more than 4 million Coptic
Orthodox Christians in Egypt. However media and other agencies, sometimes taking into account the claims of the
church itself, generally approximate the Coptic Orthodox population at 10% of the Egyptian population or 10 million
people. Egyptian Copts are the biggest Christian community in the Arab world. Estimates of their numbers vary, but
generally range between 4.7 and 7.1 million. The majority of them live in Egypt under the jurisdiction of the Coptic
Orthodox Church. Since 2006, Egyptian censuses have not reported on religion and church leaders have alleged that
Christians were under-counted in government surveys. The Coptic Church contests the accuracy of government
censuses. In 2017, a government owned newspaper <color=#3366CC>Al Ahram</color> estimated the percentage of Copts at 10 to 15% and the
membership claimed by the Coptic Orthodox Church is in the range of 20 to 25 million. In 2023, Pope Tawadros II
claimed the Coptic Orthodox Church counts 15 million members in Egypt and 2 million in the diaspora. Bishops and
Pope Shenouda III had repeatedly claimed that the population of Coptic Orthodox Christians is underreported by the
Egyptian government. Church leaders have claimed that, as of 2009, Coptic Orthodox Christians comprised up to 20%
of the population. Pew Research has estimated there were four million Egyptian 'Orthodox' Christians in 2016, primarily
Coptic Orthodox. The World Christian Database, published in 2021 and produced by the Center for the Study of Global
Christianity at the Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary, estimated that were 8,798,000 Oriental Orthodox Christians
in Egypt.
There are also significant numbers in the diaspora outside Africa in countries such as the <color=#3366CC>United States</color> (USA),
<color=#3366CC>Canada</color>, <color=#3366CC>Australia</color>, <color=#3366CC>France</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Germany</color>. The exact number of Egyptian born Coptic Orthodox Christians in the
diaspora is hard to determine and is roughly estimated to be close to 1 million. Estimates in 2013 put the total number
of Egyptians in the USA, Canada, Australia, and <color=#3366CC>Great Britain</color> at 533,000.
There are between 150,000 and 200,000 adherents in <color=#3366CC>Sudan</color>.
Jurisdiction outside Egypt
Besides Egypt, the Church of Alexandria has jurisdiction over all of <color=#3366CC>Africa</color>. The following autocephalous churches have
strong historical ties to the Coptic Orthodox Church.
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church
Tradition holds that Ethiopia was first evangelized by <color=#3366CC>St. Matthew</color> and <color=#3366CC>St. Bartholomew</color> in the 1st century AD, and the
first Ethiopian convert is thought to have been the eunuch in Jerusalem mentioned in <color=#3366CC>The Acts of the Apostles</color>
(8:27–40). Ethiopia was further Christianized in the 4th century AD by two men (likely brothers) from Tyre—St.
Frumentius. Ever since the conversion of <color=#3366CC>Ezana of Axum</color> to Christianity by Frumentius in 325 AD, the <color=#3366CC>Ethiopian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Orthodox Tewahedo Church</color> has received its archbishops from the Coptic Orthodox Church. Until the mid-twentieth
century, the metropolitans of the Ethiopian church were ethnic Copts. Joseph II consecrated Archbishop Abuna Basilios
as the first native head of the <color=#3366CC>Ethiopian Church</color> on 14 January 1951. In 1959, Pope Cyril VI of Alexandria crowned
Abuna Basilios as the first Patriarch of Ethiopia.
Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church
Following the independence of <color=#3366CC>Eritrea</color> from Ethiopia in 1993, the newly independent Eritrean government appealed to
Pope Shenouda III of Alexandria for Eritrean Orthodox autocephaly. In 1994, Pope Shenouda ordained Abune Phillipos
as first Archbishop of Eritrea.
Pope
The pope of the Coptic Orthodox Church, presently Tawadros II, function as a leader for the whole church and the
highest ranking among the church's bishops. The pope is considered the Patriarch of Alexandria and holds that the
office descends from Mark the Apostle.
Administration
The Coptic Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria is governed by its Holy Synod, which is headed by the Patriarch of
Alexandria. Under his authority are the metropolitan archbishops, metropolitan bishops, <color=#3366CC>diocesan bishops</color>, patriarchal
exarchs, missionary bishops, auxiliary bishops, suffragan bishops, assistant bishops, chorbishops and the patriarchal
vicars for the Church of Alexandria. They are organized as follows:
• 27 metropolitanates, out of which 20 metropolitanates are in Egypt, one metropolitanate in the Near East, two in
the USA, one in Africa and 3 in Europe; served by one metropolitan archbishop and 26 metropolitan bishops; out of
the 27 hierarchs, one metropolitan archbishop is in the Near East, while 20 metropolitan bishops are in Egypt, two
metropolitan bishops in the USA, one metropolitan bishop in Africa and 3 metropolitan bishops in Europe.
• 66 dioceses with 39 diocesan bishops are in Egypt, 14 diocesan bishops are in Europe, 6 diocesan bishops are in
North America, two diocesan bishops are in South America, two diocesan bishops are in Sudan, two diocesan
bishops in Australia, and one diocesan bishop in Africa.
• one suffragan diocese, with one suffragan bishop in North America.
• 5 auxiliary bishops, two in the Diocese of Los Angeles, two in the Southern USA diocese in North America and one
in the diocese of Qena, Egypt.
• 13 assistant bishops in Egypt for 13 suffragan dioceses within an archdiocese under the Patriarch's jurisdiction.
• 8 patriarchal exarchates, with one in Asia & Australia, one in Africa, three in North America and three in Egypt.
• 18 bishop abbots for 17 patriarchal monasteries in Egypt and one patriarchal monastery in Australia.
• four general bishops, administrators of patriarchal institutions in Egypt.
• one hegumen in the capacity of grand Economos, patriarchal vicar for Alexandria.
• one hegumen as administrative patriarchal vicar for Cairo.
Badger
Badgers are medium-sized short-legged <color=#3366CC>omnivores</color> in the <color=#3366CC>superfamily</color> Musteloidea. Badgers are a polyphyletic rather
than a natural taxonomic grouping, being united by their squat bodies and adaptions for fossorial activity rather than by
their ancestral relationships: Musteloidea contains several families, only two of which (the "weasel family" <color=#3366CC>Mustelidae</color>
and the "skunk family" <color=#3366CC>Mephitidae</color>) include badgers; moreover, both of these families also include various other animals
that are not badgers.
The fifteen <color=#3366CC>species</color> of mustelid badgers are grouped in four subfamilies: four species of Melinae (genera Meles and
Arctonyx) including the <color=#3366CC>European badger</color>, five species of Helictidinae (genus Melogale) or <color=#3366CC>ferret-badger</color>, the <color=#3366CC>honey</color>
<color=#3366CC>badger</color> or ratel Mellivorinae (genus Mellivora), and the <color=#3366CC>American badger</color> Taxideinae (genus Taxidea). Badgers include
the most basal mustelids; the American badger is the most basal of all, followed successively by the ratel and the
Melinae; the estimated split dates are about 17.8, 15.5 and 14.8 million years ago, respectively.
The two species of Asiatic stink badgers of the genus Mydaus were formerly included within Melinae (and thus
Mustelidae), but more recent genetic evidence indicates these are actually members of the <color=#3366CC>skunk</color> family (Mephitidae).
Badger mandibular condyles connect to long cavities in their skulls, which gives resistance to jaw dislocation and
increases their bite grip strength. This in turn limits jaw movement to hinging open and shut, or sliding from side to side,
but it does not hamper the twisting movement possible for the jaws of most <color=#3366CC>mammals</color>.
Badgers have rather short, wide bodies, with short legs for digging. They have elongated, weasel-like heads with small
ears. Their tails vary in length depending on species; the stink badger has a very short tail, while the ferret-badger's tail
can be 46 – 51 cm long, depending on age. They have black faces with distinctive white markings, grey bodies with a
light-coloured stripe from head to tail, and dark legs with light-coloured underbellies. They grow to around 90 cm in
length, including tail.
The European badger is one of the largest; the American badger, the hog badger, and the honey badger are generally
a little smaller and lighter. Stink badgers are smaller still, and ferret-badgers are the smallest of all. They weigh around
9 – 11 kg, while some Eurasian badgers weigh around 18 kg.
Etymology
The word "badger" originally applied to the <color=#3366CC>European badger</color> (Meles meles), comes from earlier bageard (16th century),
presumably referring to the white mark borne like a badge on its forehead. Similarly, a now archaic synonym was
bauson 'badger' (1375), a variant of bausond 'striped, piebald', from Old French bausant, baucent 'id.'.

The less common name brock (<color=#3366CC>Old English</color>: brocc), (<color=#3366CC>Scots</color>: brock) is a <color=#3366CC>Celtic</color> <color=#3366CC>loanword</color> (cf. Gaelic broc and <color=#3366CC>Welsh</color>
broch, from Proto-Celtic *brokkos) meaning "grey". The Proto-Germanic term was *þahsuz (cf. <color=#3366CC>German</color> Dachs, <color=#3366CC>Dutch</color>
das, <color=#3366CC>Norwegian</color> svintoks; <color=#3366CC>Early Modern English</color> dasse), probably from the <color=#3366CC>PIE</color> root *tek'- "to construct," so the badger
would have been named after its digging of setts (tunnels); the Germanic term *þahsuz became taxus or taxō, -ōnis in
<color=#3366CC>Latin</color> glosses, replacing mēlēs ("<color=#3366CC>marten</color>" or "badger"), and from these words the common <color=#3366CC>Romance</color> terms for the
animal evolved (<color=#3366CC>Italian</color> tasso, <color=#3366CC>French</color> taisson—blaireau is now more common—<color=#3366CC>Catalan</color> toixó, <color=#3366CC>Spanish</color> tejón,
<color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color> texugo).
A male European badger is a boar, a female is a sow, and a young badger is a cub. However, in North America the
young are usually called kits, while the terms male and female are generally used for adults. A collective name
suggested for a group of colonial badgers is a cete, but badger colonies are more often called clans. A badger's home
is called a sett.

Distribution
Badgers are found in much of <color=#3366CC>North America</color>, <color=#3366CC>Great Britain</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ireland</color> and most of the rest of Europe as far north as

southern <color=#3366CC>Scandinavia</color>. They live as far east as <color=#3366CC>Japan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Korea</color> and <color=#3366CC>China</color>. The Javan ferret-badger lives in <color=#3366CC>Indonesia</color>,
and the Bornean ferret-badger lives in <color=#3366CC>Malaysia</color>. The honey badger is found in most of <color=#3366CC>sub-Saharan Africa</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Arabian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Desert</color>, southern <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>, <color=#3366CC>Turkmenistan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color> and <color=#3366CC>India</color>.
Behaviour
The behaviour of badgers differs by family, but all shelter underground, living in burrows called setts, which may be
very extensive. Some are solitary, moving from home to home, while others are known to form clans called cetes. Cete
size is variable from two to 15.
Badgers can run or gallop at 25 – 30 km/h for short periods of time. Some species, notably the <color=#3366CC>honey badger</color>, can
climb well. In March 2024, scientists released footage of a wild Asian badger climbing a tree to a height of 2.5 m in
South Korea. Badgers are nocturnal.
In North America, <color=#3366CC>coyotes</color> sometimes eat badgers and vice versa, but the majority of their interactions seem to be
mutual or neutral. American badgers and coyotes have been seen hunting together in a cooperative fashion.
Diet
The diet of the Eurasian badger consists largely of <color=#3366CC>earthworms</color> (especially Lumbricus terrestris), <color=#3366CC>insects</color>, <color=#3366CC>grubs</color>, and the

eggs and young of ground-nesting <color=#3366CC>birds</color>. They also eat small <color=#3366CC>mammals</color>, <color=#3366CC>amphibians</color>, <color=#3366CC>reptiles</color> and <color=#3366CC>birds</color>, as well as <color=#3366CC>roots</color>
and <color=#3366CC>fruit</color>. They are occasional predators of domestic chickens, and are able to break into enclosures that a fox cannot.
In southern Spain, badgers feed to a significant degree on rabbits.
American badgers are fossorial <color=#3366CC>carnivores</color> – i.e. they catch a significant proportion of their food underground, by
digging. They can tunnel after ground-dwelling rodents at speed.
The honey badger of Africa consumes <color=#3366CC>honey</color>, <color=#3366CC>porcupines</color>, and even venomous <color=#3366CC>snakes</color> (such as the puff adder); they
climb trees to gain access to honey from bees' nests.
Badgers have been known to become intoxicated with <color=#3366CC>alcohol</color> after eating rotting fruit.
Relation with humans
Hunting
Hunting badgers for sport has been common in many countries. The Dachshund (German for "badger hound") dog
breed was bred for this purpose. Badger-baiting was formerly a popular <color=#3366CC>blood sport</color>. Although badgers are normally
quite docile, they fight fiercely when cornered. This led people to capture and box badgers and then wager on whether
a dog could succeed in removing the badger from its refuge. In England, opposition from naturalists led to its ban under
the Cruelty to Animals Act 1835 and the Protection of Badgers Act 1992 (c. 51) made it an offence to kill, injure, or take
a badger or to interfere with a sett unless under license from a statutory authority. The Hunting Act 2004 further banned
fox hunters from blocking setts during their chases.
Badgers have been trapped commercially for their pelts, which have been used for centuries to make shaving brushes,
a purpose to which it is particularly suited owing to its high water retention. Virtually all commercially available badger
hair now comes from mainland China, though, which has farms for the purpose. The Chinese supply three grades of
hair to domestic and foreign brush makers. Village cooperatives are also licensed by the national government to hunt
and process badgers to avoid their becoming a crop nuisance in rural northern China. The European badger is also
used as trim for some traditional Scottish clothing. The American badger is also used for paintbrushes and as trim for
some <color=#3366CC>Native American</color> garments.
Culling
Controlling the badger population is prohibited in many European countries since badgers are listed in the Berne
Convention, but they are not otherwise the subject of any international treaty or legislation. Many badgers in Europe
were gassed during the 1960s and 1970s to control <color=#3366CC>rabies</color>.
Until the 1980s, badger culling in the United Kingdom was undertaken in the form of gassing, allegedly to control the
spread of <color=#3366CC>bovine tuberculosis</color> (bTB). Limited culling resumed in 1998 as part of a 10-year randomised trial cull, which
was considered by John Krebs and others to show that culling was ineffective. Some groups called for a selective cull,
whilst others favoured a programme of vaccination. Wales and Northern Ireland are currently conducting field trials of a
badger vaccination programme. In 2012 the government authorised a limited cull led by the Department for
Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. However it was later deferred and a wide range of reasons given. In August 2013
a full culling programme began, whereby it was expected that about 5,000 badgers would be killed over six weeks in
West <color=#3366CC>Somerset</color> and <color=#3366CC>Gloucestershire</color> using a mixture of controlled shooting and free shooting (some badgers were to be
trapped in cages first). The cull caused many protests, with emotional, economic and scientific reasons being cited. The
badger is considered an iconic species of the British countryside and it has been claimed by shadow ministers that
"The government's own figures show it will cost more than it saves...", and Lord Krebs, who led the Randomised
Badger Culling Trial in the 1990s, said the two pilots "will not yield any useful information".
Badger gates
When protecting woodlands from deer and rabbit, installing fences in badger territory can be problematic. Because
badgers are persistent and strong, if fences are placed across their "runs"—established foraging and travel paths—they
may well dig through or under, damaging the fence and leaving openings that rabbits can get through. Ideally, badger
runs should be identified before fence construction begins. The gateways are constructed in stages over time to ensure
that badgers are using the manmade openings instead of damaging the new fence: starting with leaving a cut opening
in the fence at ground level, later laying a floor (threshold), later still framing the opening, and eventually hanging a
small free-swinging door that is heavy enough that rabbits don't seem to learn how to push them open. The
recommended door size is 18 by 25 cm and weighs about 1.1 kg.
With a special license, badger fencing and one-way gates may be installed to exclude resident badgers from an area
being developed.
Traditional medicine
Badgers have been used in traditional medicine in Europe, Asia and Africa.
Food
Although rarely eaten today in the United States or the United Kingdom, badgers were once a primary meat source for
the diets of Native Americans and European colonists. Badgers were also eaten in Britain during <color=#3366CC>World War II</color> and the
1950s. In some areas of Russia, the consumption of badger meat is still widespread. Shish kebabs made from badger,
along with dog meat and pork, are a major source of trichinosis outbreaks in the Altai Region of Russia. In <color=#3366CC>Croatia</color>
badger meat is rarely eaten, but when it is, it is usually smoked, dried, or served in <color=#3366CC>goulash</color>. In France, badger meat
was used in the preparation of several dishes, such as Blaireau au sang, and it was a relatively common ingredient in
countryside cuisine. Badger meat was eaten in some parts of Spain until recently.
Pets
Badgers are sometimes kept as pets. Keeping a badger as a pet or offering one for sale is an offence in the United
Kingdom under the 1992 Protection of Badgers Act.
In popular culture
Medieval European <color=#3366CC>bestiaries</color> described badgers as working together to dig holes under mountains. They were said to
lie down at the entrance of the hole holding a stick in their mouths, while other badgers piled dirt on their bellies. Two
badgers would then take hold of the stick in the badger's mouth, and drag the animal loaded with dirt away, in the
fashion of a wagon. The moralizing component of bestiaries often took precedence over their function as natural history
texts, and this description of badgers was likely understood as an allegory.
In German-speaking areas of Europe, badgers were traditionally used to predict the length of <color=#3366CC>winter</color>. This became the
North American tradition of <color=#3366CC>Groundhog Day</color>.
The 19th-century poem "The Badger" by <color=#3366CC>John Clare</color> describes a badger hunt and badger-baiting.
Many modern works of literature feature badger characters. Some of the most notable are <color=#3366CC>Kenneth Grahame</color>'s
children's novel <color=#3366CC>The Wind in the Willows</color> (1908), <color=#3366CC>Beatrix Potter</color>'s The Tale of Mr. Tod (1912), <color=#3366CC>T. H. White</color>'s The Once
and Future King (1958, written 1938–41), Fantastic Mr. Fox (1970) by <color=#3366CC>Roald Dahl</color>, Richard Adams's Watership Down
(1972), and Brian Jacques's Redwall series (1986–2011).
Badgers also feature in visual media. A Flash Video called Badgers went <color=#3366CC>viral</color> in the early years of <color=#3366CC>YouTube</color>. The 2013
<color=#3366CC>PC</color> video game Shelter has the player control a mother badger protecting her cubs.
The badger is the state animal of the U.S. state of <color=#3366CC>Wisconsin</color>, and Bucky Badger is the mascot of the University of
Wisconsin–Madison. The badger also serves as the mascot of Brock University in Ontario, Canada; The University of
Sussex and St Aidan's College, both in <color=#3366CC>England</color>; and of the Hufflepuff house of Hogwarts in the fictional <color=#3366CC>Harry Potter</color>
franchise.
Sengoku period
The Sengoku period (Sengoku jidai) was an era of civil war, political fragmentation and social change in <color=#3366CC>Japanese</color>
<color=#3366CC>history</color>. It conventionally began with the Ōnin War in 1467, although the Kyōtoku incident of 1454 and the Meiō incident
of 1493 have also been proposed as starting points. Its end is variously dated to <color=#3366CC>Oda Nobunaga</color>'s entry into <color=#3366CC>Kyoto</color> in
1568, the fall of the Ashikaga shogunate in 1573, <color=#3366CC>Toyotomi Hideyoshi</color>'s unification of Japan in 1590, the <color=#3366CC>Battle of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Sekigahara</color> in 1600 or the Siege of Osaka in 1615. The period overlaps with the later <color=#3366CC>Muromachi period</color> and, under
broader definitions, the Azuchi–Momoyama period.
The Ōnin War devastated much of Kyoto and accelerated the decline of the Ashikaga shogunate. Although the
Ashikaga shōguns remained in office until 1573, their ability to control the provinces became increasingly limited.
Provincial governors, their deputies and local warrior families established autonomous regional regimes. The most
successful rulers, known as sengoku daimyō, built castles and castle towns, conducted land surveys, issued territorial
laws and organized warriors more directly under their authority.
The period is associated with gekokujō, or "the low overthrowing the high", as retainers displaced their lords and junior
branches contested control of warrior families. It also saw the growth of armed leagues known as ikki, including village
and provincial associations as well as the Buddhist Ikkō-ikki. These developments did not eliminate established social
distinctions, but they created opportunities for figures such as Hōjō Sōun, Saitō Dōsan and <color=#3366CC>Toyotomi Hideyoshi</color> to rise
from comparatively modest positions.
The Sengoku period also experienced expanding trade, the growth of castle towns and increased contact with
Europeans. Portuguese merchants introduced the arquebus in 1543, after which Japanese weapons manufacturers
began producing firearms domestically. The arrival of <color=#3366CC>Francis Xavier</color> in 1549 was followed by the spread of Christianity,
particularly in parts of <color=#3366CC>Kyushu</color>.
Nobunaga entered Kyoto in 1568 and ended the Ashikaga shogunate five years later. After his death in 1582,
Hideyoshi continued the process of consolidation and brought the remaining major regional powers under his authority
by 1590. Following Hideyoshi's death, <color=#3366CC>Tokugawa Ieyasu</color> defeated his principal rivals at Sekigahara, became <color=#3366CC>shōgun</color> in
1603 and destroyed the Toyotomi house in 1615. Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu are therefore commonly called
Japan's "Three Great Unifiers", although political unification was a prolonged process involving many regional rulers
and institutions.
Background
The emperor remained the formal sovereign and an important source of political legitimacy during the <color=#3366CC>Muromachi</color>
<color=#3366CC>period</color>, but effective military government was exercised by the Ashikaga shogunate in Kyoto. The imperial court
continued to perform religious and ceremonial functions, confer titles and ranks, and participate in political affairs; it did
not simply delegate all authority to the <color=#3366CC>shōgun</color>. The Ashikaga government depended upon cooperation among the
shōgun, court nobles, religious institutions and regional military families.
In the provinces, the shogunate governed principally through military governors known as shugo. Their original
responsibilities included policing, suppressing rebellion, and mobilizing warriors, but their authority expanded during the
14th century to include greater jurisdiction over land disputes and taxation. During the Nanboku-chō period, the
emergency hanzei system permitted military authorities to divert part of the income from specified estates to support
armies. It was not a general authorization for every shugo to collect half of all taxes within a province. Over time, some
shugo used their military, judicial, and fiscal powers to organize local warriors into retainer bands and increase their
control over provincial land and revenue. The most powerful became known as shugo daimyō, although their authority
continued to depend partly upon appointment by the shogunate and cooperation with provincial warriors, estate
proprietors, temples and local communities.
Ashikaga authority reached its greatest extent under the third shōgun, Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, who secured the
reunification of the Northern and Southern imperial courts in 1392 and compelled many leading military families to
recognize his supremacy. His son Ashikaga Yoshimochi maintained much of this authority, but a succession crisis
followed the death of Yoshimochi's son, Ashikaga Yoshikazu, in 1425. When Yoshimochi died without a surviving heir
in 1428, senior officials selected the next shōgun by lot from among four of Yoshimitsu's sons who had entered
religious life. The chosen candidate returned to secular life as Ashikaga Yoshinori.
Yoshinori attempted to strengthen shogunal control by intervening in the successions of powerful families, suppressing
regional opponents, and confiscating or reallocating estates. These policies restored the shōgun's personal authority
but also generated hostility among some leading warriors. In 1441, Akamatsu Mitsusuke assassinated Yoshinori during
a banquet in what became known as the Kakitsu incident. The Akamatsu uprising was subsequently defeated, but
Yoshinori was succeeded by his eight-year-old son Ashikaga Yoshikatsu, who died two years later, and then by
Yoshikatsu's younger brother Ashikaga Yoshimasa. The succession of child shōguns increased the influence of senior
shogunal officials and powerful shugo daimyō.
During Yoshimasa's administration, disputes within the Hatakeyama and Shiba families became entangled with the
rivalry between Hosokawa Katsumoto and Yamana Sōzen, two of the most powerful military leaders in Kyoto.
Uncertainty over the shogunal succession further complicated these conflicts after Yoshimasa first designated his
brother Ashikaga Yoshimi as his heir and his wife Hino Tomiko subsequently gave birth to Ashikaga Yoshihisa. These
overlapping disputes divided major military families into opposing coalitions and contributed to the outbreak of the Ōnin
War in 1467.
Beginning of the Sengoku period
Historians do not agree on a single event that marks the beginning of the Sengoku period. The traditional starting date
is the outbreak of the Ōnin War in 1467, because the conflict severely weakened the political order centered on the
Ashikaga shogunate in Kyoto. Other interpretations begin with the Kyōtoku incident in 1454, which initiated decades of
warfare in the <color=#3366CC>Kantō region</color>, or the Meiō incident in 1493, after which powerful military families repeatedly deposed,
installed, and competed for control of Ashikaga shōguns.
The Kyōtoku incident began when Ashikaga Shigeuji, the Kantō kubō and principal Ashikaga authority in eastern
Japan, ordered the killing of his deputy, Kantō kanrei Uesugi Noritada, in 1454. The murder divided the warrior families
of the Kantō between Shigeuji and the Uesugi-led coalition supported by the Kyoto shogunate. Shigeuji withdrew to
Koga, from which he and his successors became known as the Koga kubō, while the shogunate established a
competing Ashikaga authority at Horigoe. Although a settlement was reached in 1482, the conflict left the Kantō
politically divided and is therefore sometimes treated as the regional beginning of the Sengoku period.
The Ōnin War grew from several interconnected disputes rather than from the Ashikaga succession alone. Rival
branches of the Hatakeyama and Shiba families contested their respective leaderships, while Hosokawa Katsumoto
and Yamana Sōzen competed for influence within the shogunate. The uncertain succession of Shōgun Ashikaga
Yoshimasa, involving his brother Ashikaga Yoshimi and infant son Ashikaga Yoshihisa, became entangled with these
existing rivalries. By 1467, the competing groups had assembled large armies in Kyoto under coalitions conventionally
known as the Eastern and Western armies.
Fighting destroyed large portions of Kyoto but produced no decisive victor. The alliances were not fixed: participants
changed sides, pursued local disputes, and continued fighting after Katsumoto and Sōzen both died in 1473. Warfare
also spread beyond the capital as leading families fought over provincial successions and control of estates. The
conflict in Kyoto ended in 1477 when Ōuchi Masahiro and the remaining Western forces departed, but the disputes that
had fueled it were not resolved.
The Ōnin War did not immediately eliminate either the Ashikaga shogunate or every established provincial government.
It instead accelerated an uneven process of political decentralization. Some shugo returned to their provinces and
strengthened their territorial authority, while others lost power to deputy governors known as shugodai, provincial
warriors known as kokujin, or rival branches of their own families. Local communities and religious organizations also
formed leagues called ikki, including the provincial league that governed southern Yamashiro Province after 1485 and
the Ikkō-ikki that took control of Kaga Province in 1488.
The regional rulers later described as sengoku daimyō emerged gradually from several different backgrounds. Some
descended from established shugo families, while others were former shugodai, kokujin or retainers who displaced
their superiors. What distinguished them was not simply the absence of a shogunal appointment, but their ability to
exercise comparatively direct military, judicial and fiscal authority over a defined territory. Even then, their power
depended upon alliances with subordinate warriors, villages, temples and commercial communities.
Some recent scholarship, particularly in Japan, places the beginning of the Sengoku period at the 1493 Meiō incident.
While Shōgun Ashikaga Yoshitane was campaigning against Hatakeyama Yoshitoyo, kanrei Hosokawa Masamoto
seized Kyoto, removed Yoshitane, and installed Ashikaga Yoshizumi as shōgun. Yoshitane escaped and continued to
claim the office, producing rival shogunal lines supported by competing military coalitions. From this interpretation, the
Meiō incident was more decisive than the Ōnin War because it demonstrated that a leading retainer could depose a
reigning shōgun and made control of the shogunate itself an object of prolonged military competition.
History
Start and end dates
Because the Sengoku period was a gradual breakdown and reconstruction of political authority rather than a formally
proclaimed era, historians use different beginning and ending dates. The Kyōtoku incident of 1454 is sometimes used
because it began prolonged warfare and divided Ashikaga authority in the <color=#3366CC>Kantō region</color>. The conventional date is 1467,
when the Ōnin War began in Kyoto, while another interpretation favors the Meiō incident of 1493, when Hosokawa
Masamoto deposed Shōgun Ashikaga Yoshitane and installed Ashikaga Yoshizumi.
An early ending date is 1568, when <color=#3366CC>Oda Nobunaga</color> entered Kyoto and installed Ashikaga Yoshiaki as shōgun. This
date conventionally marks the beginning of the Azuchi–Momoyama period, but it did not end either the Ashikaga
shogunate or warfare among the regional daimyō. The year 1573, when Nobunaga expelled Yoshiaki from Kyoto, is
used when the end of the Sengoku period is equated with the termination of the Ashikaga shogunate and the
<color=#3366CC>Muromachi period</color>. Nobunaga's move to Azuchi Castle in 1576 is another proposed transition point because it gave the
later Azuchi–Momoyama period part of its name.
Another group of dates associates the period's end with the political unification of Japan. In 1587, <color=#3366CC>Toyotomi Hideyoshi</color>
issued the sōbujirei, which prohibited daimyō from conducting private wars. His defeat of the Later Hōjō clan in the
Odawara campaign of 1590 brought the last major independent regional power under his authority and is frequently
treated as the completion of national unification. Hideyoshi's death in 1598 reopened the struggle for national
supremacy, however, making 1590 an unsuitable endpoint for definitions that include the subsequent conflict between
the Toyotomi and Tokugawa coalitions.
Later ending dates focus upon the establishment of Tokugawa rule. <color=#3366CC>Tokugawa Ieyasu</color> defeated his principal rivals at
the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 and was appointed <color=#3366CC>shōgun</color> in 1603, establishing the <color=#3366CC>Tokugawa shogunate</color>. The
Toyotomi family nevertheless retained substantial autonomy at Osaka Castle until its destruction in the Siege of Osaka
in 1615. Consequently, 1600 represents Tokugawa military supremacy, 1603 the institutional foundation of the new
shogunate and 1615 the elimination of its last major rival.
The Sengoku and Azuchi–Momoyama periods therefore overlap under many systems of periodization. The latter
generally describes the governments and unification campaigns of Nobunaga and Hideyoshi, beginning in 1568, 1573
or 1576 and ending with Hideyoshi's death, Sekigahara or the establishment of the Tokugawa shogunate. It should not
always be understood as a wholly separate period beginning only after the Sengoku period had ended.
Hosokawa dominance of the Ashikaga shogunate
After the death of the ninth shōgun, Ashikaga Yoshihisa, in 1489, his cousin Ashikaga Yoshitane succeeded him as the
tenth shōgun. Yoshitane supported Hatakeyama Masanaga in the continuing succession conflict within the
Hatakeyama clan, but their policies brought them into opposition with kanrei Hosokawa Masamoto. While Yoshitane
and Masanaga were campaigning against Hatakeyama Yoshitoyo in Kawachi Province in 1493, Masamoto seized
control of Kyoto in the Meiō incident. Yoshitane was deposed and replaced by Ashikaga Yoshizumi, while Masanaga
was defeated and killed. Yoshitane escaped captivity and continued to claim the shogunate, creating two rival Ashikaga
lines supported by competing military coalitions.
As kanrei, Masamoto had been one of the shogunate's most senior officials, but his power after 1493 extended beyond
the customary authority of that office. He controlled the government in Kyoto and exercised decisive influence over
Yoshizumi's early administration. The kanrei is sometimes compared with the shikken of the earlier <color=#3366CC>Kamakura</color>
<color=#3366CC>shogunate</color>, but the two offices developed in different political systems and were not direct equivalents. Masamoto's
deposition of a reigning shōgun was a major break with established practice and is one reason that some historians
use the Meiō incident as the beginning of the Sengoku period.
Masamoto had no biological children and adopted three prospective heirs from different families: Hosokawa Sumiyuki,
originally a son of the aristocratic Kujō family; Hosokawa Sumimoto, from the Awa branch of the Hosokawa; and
Hosokawa Takakuni, from another collateral branch. Masamoto initially favored Sumiyuki but later designated
Sumimoto as his successor. In 1507, retainers supporting the disinherited Sumiyuki assassinated Masamoto in an
event known as the Eishō disturbance (Eishō no sakuran). Sumiyuki did not personally kill Masamoto and did not retain
power for long; supporters of Sumimoto and Takakuni defeated and killed him several weeks later.
The alliance between Sumimoto and Takakuni soon collapsed. In 1508, Takakuni joined former shōgun Yoshitane and
Ōuchi Yoshioki, whose army advanced on Kyoto from western Japan. Yoshizumi and Sumimoto were driven from the
capital, Yoshitane was restored as shōgun and Takakuni became the dominant Hosokawa leader in Kyoto. Fighting
continued between the rival Yoshitane–Takakuni and Yoshizumi–Sumimoto coalitions, including the Battle of
Funaokayama in 1511. After Yoshioki returned to his western provinces in 1518 and Sumimoto died in 1520, Takakuni
exercised increased control over the shogunate. When Yoshitane broke with him in 1521, Takakuni installed
Yoshizumi's son Ashikaga Yoshiharu as the twelfth shōgun.
Sumimoto's son Hosokawa Harumoto, supported by Miyoshi Motonaga, renewed the struggle against Takakuni. Their
forces expelled Takakuni and Yoshiharu from Kyoto in 1527, although control of the capital continued to change hands.
Takakuni subsequently allied with Uragami Muramune, but their coalition was defeated by Harumoto and Motonaga at
the Battle of Daimotsu in 1531. Takakuni and Muramune were both killed, leaving Harumoto as the principal Hosokawa
power in the central provinces.
Harumoto soon came to regard Motonaga's growing military influence as a threat. In 1532, he encouraged armed
adherents of the Ikkō-shū to attack Motonaga, who was defeated and forced to kill himself at <color=#3366CC>Sakai</color>. The resulting
Ikkō-ikki mobilization expanded beyond Harumoto's control and produced further warfare around Kyoto and Osaka.
Although Harumoto temporarily dominated the shogunate, his dependence upon powerful retainers anticipated the
subsequent rise of Motonaga's son, Miyoshi Nagayoshi.
Other regions
Chūgoku region (Mōri Motonari)
<color=#3366CC>Mōri Motonari</color> transformed the Mōri from a relatively small local warrior family in Aki Province into the dominant military
power of western <color=#3366CC>Honshu</color>. The Mōri initially operated between the much larger Ōuchi clan, based in Suō and Nagato,
and the Amago clan, based in Izumo. Motonari gained an early military reputation at the Battle of Arita-Nakaide in 1517
and became head of the Mōri clan in 1523 following the death of his young nephew. The battle was later compared with
the Battle of Okehazama because Motonari defeated a larger Aki-Takeda force, but the description “Okehazama of the
West” is a retrospective nickname rather than a contemporary name for the battle.
Motonari initially cooperated with the Amago but transferred his allegiance to the Ōuchi in 1525. During the following
years he consolidated his position among the local warrior families of Aki. His survival depended partly upon Ōuchi
support: when Amago Haruhisa invaded Aki and besieged Motonari at Yoshida-Kōriyama Castle in 1540, an Ōuchi
relief army helped force the Amago withdrawal in January 1541. The victory substantially increased the Mōri clan's
influence in Aki, but Motonari did not yet independently rule Aki, Iwami and Bingo as the previous version of this section
stated.
Motonari strengthened his position through marriage, adoption and alliances as well as warfare. His eldest son, Mōri
Takamoto, became heir to the main Mōri house, while his second and third sons were adopted into two important Aki
families as Kikkawa Motoharu and Kobayakawa Takakage. The cooperation of the Mōri, Kikkawa and Kobayakawa
houses gave the clan access to additional territory, soldiers and naval forces. The well-known “lesson of the three
arrows”, in which Motonari supposedly demonstrated to his sons that three arrows bound together could not easily be
broken, is a later legend. It reflects Motonari's documented insistence upon cooperation among his sons but is not
known to have occurred as popularly described.
The political balance in western Japan changed in 1551 when Sue Harukata, a senior Ōuchi retainer, overthrew Ōuchi
Yoshitaka in the Tainei-ji incident and installed Ōuchi Yoshinaga as the clan's nominal head. Motonari initially
maintained relations with the new regime but broke with Sue in 1554. In the Battle of Itsukushima in 1555, Mōri forces
defeated Sue's larger army and Sue killed himself. The defeat destroyed the military foundation of Yoshinaga's
government. Mōri forces then advanced into the eastern Ōuchi territories, and Yoshinaga was forced to kill himself in
1557. The collapse did not transfer the entire Ōuchi realm to Motonari: the Mōri took its eastern territories, while the
Ōtomo clan extended its influence over parts of the west and northern Kyushu.
After defeating Sue and the Ōuchi, Motonari concentrated on the Amago. Mōri forces gradually isolated the Amago
stronghold of Gassantoda Castle, which surrendered in 1566 after an extended campaign. This established Mōri
predominance across most of the Chūgoku region, although their authority remained contested by Amago restoration
forces and by the Ōtomo in northern Kyushu. The Mōri consequently developed into a regional coalition rather than
simply “pacifying” every province under uncontested personal rule.
Motonari formally transferred the clan leadership to Takamoto but continued to direct major political and military
decisions. After Takamoto's death in 1563, Motonari supported his grandson Mōri Terumoto as heir while Motoharu and
Takakage assumed leading military and administrative roles. Motonari died at Yoshida-Kōriyama Castle in 1571 at the
age of 74. He left the Mōri as one of Japan's most powerful regional houses, controlling much of western Honshu and
competing for influence in northern Kyushu.
Hokuriku, Kantō and Chūbu regions (Uesugi Kenshin)
The political order of eastern Japan had already been weakened by the conflicts between the Kantō kubō, the Uesugi
clan and other regional families. In 1546, Hōjō Ujiyasu defeated a coalition led by Uesugi Norimasa and Uesugi
Tomosada in the Battle of Kawagoe. Tomosada was killed and Norimasa was eventually driven from Kōzuke Province,
allowing the Later Hōjō clan to become the leading power in much of the <color=#3366CC>Kantō region</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Uesugi Kenshin</color> was born Nagao Kagetora and belonged to the Nagao family, hereditary deputies of the Uesugi
governors of Echigo Province. He replaced his elder brother Nagao Harukage as head of the Nagao in 1548 and
gradually consolidated his authority among Echigo's frequently divided warrior families. Describing this process as the
complete “unification” of Echigo in 1551 is misleading, because Kenshin continued to face resistance and negotiate
with powerful local retainers throughout his rule. His government also depended upon control of commerce, ports,
textile production and transportation networks rather than upon military conquest alone.
Uesugi Norimasa sought refuge with Kagetora after his defeat by the Later Hōjō and encouraged him to intervene in
the Kantō. In 1559, Kagetora travelled to Kyoto, where he received an audience with Shōgun Ashikaga Yoshiteru and
visited the imperial court. He launched a large Kantō campaign in 1560–1561, gaining the temporary submission of
numerous regional lords and advancing to the Hōjō capital at Odawara Castle. Although his army burned parts of the
castle town, it did not capture the fortress, and many of the alliances assembled during the campaign proved
temporary.
In 1561, Norimasa adopted Kagetora into the Uesugi clan and transferred to him the Uesugi family name and claim to
the office of Kantō kanrei. The succession was ceremonially recognized at Tsurugaoka Hachimangū in Kamakura.
Kagetora subsequently used several names, including Uesugi Masatora and Terutora, before becoming best known by
his Buddhist name, Kenshin. He continued campaigning in the Kantō during the 1560s, but the Later Hōjō recovered
much of the territory that had temporarily submitted to him. Kenshin and Ujiyasu concluded an alliance in 1569 in
response to their common conflict with <color=#3366CC>Takeda Shingen</color>, although the agreement did not permanently settle their
territorial rivalry.
Kenshin's rivalry with Shingen developed from Takeda expansion into northern Shinano Province, where displaced
local lords requested Kenshin's assistance. Their armies confronted one another during five campaigns around
Kawanakajima in 1553, 1555, 1557, 1561 and 1564. These encounters are conventionally called the Battles of
Kawanakajima, but most consisted principally of manoeuvring, sieges or limited skirmishing. Only the fourth campaign
in 1561 produced a major pitched battle. It inflicted heavy casualties on both armies but did not result in a decisive or
lasting territorial settlement.
During the 1570s, Kenshin increasingly concentrated upon the Hokuriku region. His forces expanded through Etchū
Province and intervened in a succession conflict within the Noto Hatakeyama clan. After a prolonged campaign, Nanao
Castle fell to the Uesugi in 1577, bringing most of Noto Province under Kenshin's authority. This expansion brought him
into direct conflict with forces commanded by retainers of <color=#3366CC>Oda Nobunaga</color>. Later accounts describe the subsequent
Battle of Tedorigawa as a major Uesugi victory, but the size of the armies, course of the fighting and extent of the Oda
defeat are uncertain. It is therefore safer to state that the Oda army withdrew after confronting Uesugi forces than to
claim that Kenshin decisively defeated Nobunaga personally.
Kenshin died suddenly at Kasugayama Castle in 1578 at the age of 48 under Western age reckoning, or 49 under the
traditional Japanese system. His death is commonly attributed to a stroke or cerebral hemorrhage, but the surviving
evidence does not establish a definitive medical diagnosis. Because he left no biological children and had not secured
an uncontested successor, his adopted sons Uesugi Kagekatsu and Uesugi Kagetora fought for control of the clan in
the Otate conflict, severely weakening the regional position Kenshin had constructed.
Firearms, warfare, and social change
According to the traditional account, Portuguese merchants introduced the European <color=#3366CC>matchlock</color> arquebus to
<color=#3366CC>Tanegashima</color> in 1543. Earlier forms of gunpowder weaponry were already known in Japan, and some historians have
suggested that matchlocks from other parts of Asia may have arrived before 1543. Nevertheless, the weapons acquired
at Tanegashima provided the model for the Japanese firearm commonly called the tanegashima. Japanese craftsmen
quickly reproduced the weapon, and manufacturing centers had developed at Negoro, <color=#3366CC>Sakai</color> and Kunitomo by the
middle of the 1540s.
Matchlocks spread rapidly among the armies of the daimyō. They were commonly issued to organized groups of
infantry and were used alongside bows and spears rather than immediately replacing them. Their effectiveness
depended upon more than possession of the weapons: commanders also required trained gunners, gunsmiths,
ammunition and reliable supplies of lead and <color=#3366CC>saltpeter</color>. Consequently, firearms increased the military importance of
production centers, merchants and regional trade networks.
The adoption of firearms formed part of a broader expansion and reorganization of Sengoku armies, but it did not by
itself create the ashigaru or cause the consolidation of Japan. Foot soldiers had played an important role before the
introduction of the matchlock, and samurai as well as common soldiers used firearms. Larger armies and more
centralized domains also depended on developments in taxation, castle construction, transportation, commerce and the
administration of vassals. Firearms nevertheless favored lords capable of mobilizing substantial financial and logistical
resources and contributed to the increasing size and complexity of late sixteenth-century warfare.
<color=#3366CC>Oda Nobunaga</color> became particularly associated with the organized battlefield use of firearms, most famously at the
Battle of Nagashino in 1575. The allied Oda and Tokugawa army used matchlock troops and field fortifications against
the attacking Takeda forces. Later accounts credited Nobunaga with deploying 3,000 gunners in rotating ranks, but the
scale and tactical novelty of this arrangement are disputed. Recent scholarship concludes that Nobunaga probably
possessed fewer firearms than later narratives claimed and that the evidence does not establish the celebrated system
of continuous rotating volleys. Nagashino was therefore an important large-scale use of matchlocks in the field, rather
than the first use of firearms in Japan or a single revolutionary event that transformed Japanese warfare.
Oda Nobunaga
<color=#3366CC>Oda Nobunaga</color> emerged as a major power after unifying most of Owari Province and defeating the substantially larger
army of Imagawa Yoshimoto at the Battle of Okehazama in 1560. He subsequently conquered Mino Province,
established his headquarters at Gifu Castle and adopted the seal Tenka Fubu, commonly interpreted as expressing his
intention to bring the realm under military authority. His control of Owari and Mino provided the territorial and economic
base from which he could intervene in the politically important Kinai region.
In 1568, Nobunaga marched to Kyoto in support of Ashikaga Yoshiaki, brother of the murdered shogun Ashikaga
Yoshiteru. After overcoming the Rokkaku clan and driving the Miyoshi forces from the capital, Nobunaga secured
Yoshiaki's installation as the fifteenth and final shogun of the Ashikaga shogunate. Although Yoshiaki provided
Nobunaga with political legitimacy, their relationship deteriorated as Nobunaga restricted the shogun's independent
authority. Yoshiaki eventually joined a coalition of Nobunaga's enemies. Nobunaga defeated him at Makishima Castle
and expelled him from Kyoto in 1573, effectively ending the Ashikaga shogunate, although Yoshiaki continued to claim
the title of shogun until 1588.
Nobunaga faced a series of overlapping conflicts rather than an uninterrupted succession of victories. His 1570
invasion of Echizen Province was abandoned after his brother-in-law Azai Nagamasa allied with Asakura Yoshikage
and threatened the Oda army's route of retreat. Nobunaga and <color=#3366CC>Tokugawa Ieyasu</color> defeated the Azai–Asakura army at
the Battle of Anegawa later that year, but the two clans continued resisting until 1573. Nobunaga then destroyed the
Asakura stronghold at Ichijōdani and forced Yoshikage to commit suicide before capturing Odani Castle, where
Nagamasa also died.
Resistance from Buddhist institutions and leagues of armed believers presented a longer challenge. Nobunaga
conducted three campaigns against the Ikkō-ikki strongholds at Nagashima, finally destroying them in 1574. The war
against Ishiyama Hongan-ji, led by Kennyo, lasted from 1570 until a negotiated evacuation of the fortress in 1580. The
Hongan-ji received assistance from several of Nobunaga's enemies, particularly the Mōri clan, whose naval forces
initially prevented the Oda from completely blockading the fortress.
In 1575, Nobunaga and Ieyasu defeated Takeda Katsuyori at the Battle of Nagashino. Matchlock troops and field
fortifications contributed to the victory, although later accounts probably exaggerated both the number of firearms and
Nobunaga's alleged use of continuous rotating volleys. Nobunaga later ordered campaigns conducted by his principal
commanders: Shibata Katsuie expanded Oda authority in the Hokuriku region, <color=#3366CC>Hashiba Hideyoshi</color> advanced against
the Mōri in western Honshu and Akechi Mitsuhide campaigned in Tamba Province. Nobunaga also constructed Azuchi
Castle, which became the administrative and symbolic center of his expanding regime.
By 1582, Nobunaga directly governed central Japan and exercised authority over a wider coalition of subordinate lords,
but he had not yet unified the entire country. The Mōri remained powerful in western Honshu, the Uesugi controlled
territory in the north and the Chōsokabe, Shimazu and Later Hōjō remained independent. During the final campaign
against the Takeda clan, Oda forces conquered Kai and Shinano and Katsuyori committed suicide. Later that year,
while staying at Honnō-ji in Kyoto with only a small entourage, Nobunaga was attacked by Akechi Mitsuhide. He died
during the Honnō-ji Incident on June 21, 1582. Hideyoshi subsequently defeated Mitsuhide and continued the process
of unification begun under Nobunaga.
Toyotomi (Hashiba) Hideyoshi
<color=#3366CC>Toyotomi Hideyoshi</color>, then known as Hashiba Hideyoshi, rose from an obscure family in Owari Province to become one
of <color=#3366CC>Oda Nobunaga</color>'s principal commanders. Later accounts described him as the son of a peasant and an ordinary
ashigaru, although the surviving evidence concerning his early life is limited and partly legendary. Under Nobunaga,
Hideyoshi participated in campaigns in central Japan and was subsequently placed in command of the Oda advance
against the Mōri clan in western Honshu.
When Nobunaga was killed by Akechi Mitsuhide in the Honnō-ji Incident in June 1582, Hideyoshi was besieging Bitchū
Takamatsu Castle. He rapidly concluded a peace with the Mōri, concealed Nobunaga's death from them until
negotiations were complete and marched his army eastward. He defeated Mitsuhide at the Battle of Yamazaki eleven
days after Nobunaga's death. At the subsequent Kiyosu Conference, Hideyoshi supported Nobunaga's infant grandson
Sambōshi as the formal Oda heir while distributing the former ruler's territories among the leading Oda retainers. This
arrangement increased Hideyoshi's influence but did not immediately make him Nobunaga's undisputed successor.
Hideyoshi's principal rival within the former Oda regime was Shibata Katsuie, who supported Nobunaga's son Oda
Nobutaka. Hideyoshi defeated their coalition at the Battle of Shizugatake in 1583, after which Katsuie and Nobutaka
committed suicide. He began constructing Osaka Castle that year on the former site of Ishiyama Hongan-ji, making it
